strengths: Addresses a genuinely open and practically important question: the adversarial robustness of deep noise suppression (DNS) models, a widely deployed class of models, filling a clear gap relative to prior work (e.g., Dong et al.) which used perceptible perturbations, only untargeted attacks, and a narrow set of environmental conditions.

Comprehensive experimental scope: four diverse models (time-domain and TF-domain, 2.26M-33.5M parameters), white-box and transfer threat models, untargeted/targeted attacks, universal perturbations, simulated over-the-air attacks with RIR convolution, and multiple SNR/reverb settings across 20 seeds.

Careful perceptibility methodology: psychoacoustic masking with meaningful enhancements (temporal pre/post-masking, 12 dB threshold tightening), which is a more defensible imperceptibility constraint than the p-norm constraints used in closest prior work.

Well-motivated metric choices with a thoughtful critique of MSE, PESQ (licensing), and DNN-based metrics (including the interesting empirical finding that optimizing against deep metrics induces metric-specific adversarial noise), supported by multi-metric evaluation (STOI, ViSQOL, NISQA, DNSMOS, Whisper WER).

Honest and thorough limitations section (no ABX user study, gradient-dependence, unsuccessful model transfer, exploding gradients in FSN+ as a pseudo-defense), plus useful negative results (no transfer even between checkpoints of the same architecture; UAPs ineffective while imperceptible).
Good reproducibility posture: public checkpoints, standard datasets, online samples, and detailed appendices covering masking computation, projection, and over-the-air optimization.
weaknesses: The core attack methodology is largely a straightforward adaptation of established techniques (PGD + MP3-style psychoacoustic masking from Schönherr et al. and Qin et al.) to a new model class; the technical novelty is modest and lies mainly in the new domain and the perceptibility enhancements.

The central 'imperceptible' claim is not validated by any human listening study (ABX or otherwise); it rests entirely on masking thresholds, and even these are loosened to 6 dB in the over-the-air setting where the authors concede audible crackling, weakening a headline claim.

Targeted attack results are weakened by the authors' own admission that STOI is unreliable as a maximization objective—audibly the outputs contain only 'a faint robotic hint of the target speech'—so claims that targeted attacks are 'near-term plausible' are stronger than the evidence supports.

No gradient-free black-box attacks are evaluated, yet the paper draws conclusions about attacker requirements; combined with total transfer failure, the practical threat model remains narrow (white-box only).

The defense evaluation is minimal: only a single non-adaptive Gaussian-noise defense, explicitly without adaptive attacks, despite the authors themselves citing that adaptive attacks would likely defeat it.

Evaluation is limited to English read speech, 5-10 second clips, and one benchmark dataset, with no generative/large-scale or streaming setting; some conclusions (e.g., OTA feasibility) rest on simulation rather than real recordings.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated research question: DNS/speech enhancement models are deployed in high-stakes applications (videoconferencing, ASR front-ends, hearing aids) yet have received little adversarial robustness scrutiny; the paper clearly positions itself against the closest prior work (Dong et al.) and identifies concrete gaps it fills (imperceptibility, minimal-noise settings, targeted attacks, reverb, over-the-air).

Broad and well-organized empirical study: four recent open-source DNS models spanning time-domain and TF-domain architectures, multiple SNR levels with/without reverberation, white-box and transfer threat models, targeted and untargeted attacks, UAPs, a simple defense, and simulated over-the-air scenarios, with 20 seeds and error bars.

Careful treatment of perceptibility constraints: builds on established psychoacoustic masking models with documented enhancements (pre/post-masking, 12 dB threshold reduction), and honestly reports where the constraint had to be loosened (6 dB in the OTA setting) and that some crackling became audible.

Technically thorough optimization methodology, including non-trivial solutions for the over-the-air projection problem (Wiener deconvolution, gradient-based projection, combined), well documented in appendices.

Honest, nuanced reporting: the paper explicitly acknowledges that targeted attacks do not yet produce perceptually intelligible target speech, that FSN+'s apparent robustness is pseudo-robustness from exploding gradients rather than a real defense, and that Gaussian noise defense is evaluated without adaptive attacks.

Thoughtful discussion of metric choices (why STOI over MSE/PESQ/DNN-based metrics) with empirical justification, and evaluation with multiple complementary metrics (ViSQOL, NISQA, DNSMOS, Whisper WER).
weaknesses: The central claim of 'imperceptible' attacks is not validated by any human study. No ABX/listening test is conducted, yet imperceptibility is the crux of the paper's contribution. This is acknowledged as a limitation, but for a paper whose headline result is imperceptible attacks rendering DNS models to gibberish, the absence of perceptual validation substantially weakens the central claim — prior work cited by the authors itself showed psychoacoustically masked perturbations to be perceptible in many cases.

Limited methodological novelty: the attack machinery (PGD + MP3-style psychoacoustic masking + STOI loss) is largely assembled from prior work (Qin et al., Schönherr et al., Madry et al.). The contribution is primarily an empirical application to a new domain rather than a new technique, which limits impact for a top-tier venue.

Targeted attacks — arguably the most security-relevant threat — do not actually succeed in a perceptually meaningful way: outputs with STOI > 0.5 w.r.t. the target contain at most 'a faint robotic hint' of target speech. The paper still frames targeted attacks as 'may soon be feasible,' which is a claim stronger than the evidence.
The over-the-air result comes at the cost of a weaker perceptibility constraint (6 dB vs. 12 dB) with admitted audible artifacts, further blurring the 'imperceptible' framing of the headline results.

Defense evaluation is shallow: only Gaussian noise is tested, without adaptive attacks, and the authors themselves note this is insufficient. No comparison against established defenses (randomized smoothing, purification, detection) that the related-work section surveys.

Analysis of why models differ in robustness is thin: the FSN+ result is attributed to exploding gradients, but no deeper investigation (e.g., adversarial training experiments, architectural ablations) explains susceptibility or points toward principled countermeasures.

Some experimental choices appear potentially favorable to the attacker and are not ablated: per-model iteration budgets normalized by wall-clock rather than convergence, best-of-run perturbation selection, English-only read speech from a single dataset, and five-second clips for one model versus ten for others.

The comparison to image denoising vulnerability (question a) rests on qualitative statements about prior work rather than any controlled cross-domain experiment, making the 'far more fragile than image denoising models' claim only loosely supported.

strengths: Addresses a clear and timely gap: systematic study of imperceptible adversarial attacks on deep noise suppression (DNS) models, which prior work (Dong et al.) left largely open with perceptible, untargeted, limited-setting attacks.

Comprehensive experimental scope: four diverse models (varying architecture, domain, parameter count), both targeted and untargeted attacks, white-box and transfer-based black-box threat models, multiple SNR/reverb settings, simulated over-the-air attacks, and universal perturbations — directly answering eight well-articulated research questions.

Methodologically careful: uses psychoacoustic masking constraints (stricter than prior work by 12 dB), principled handling of the difficult over-the-air projection problem (Wiener deconvolution + gradient-based projection), and thoughtful discussion of why STOI is preferred over MSE/PESQ/DNN metrics, including their failure modes.
Honest and thorough limitations section (no ABX study, white-box reliance, non-adaptive defense evaluation, discrete-token models untested), which increases trust in the reported findings.

Interesting negative/nuanced results: attacks do not transfer even between checkpoints of the same architecture; FSN+'s apparent robustness traced to exploding gradients (pseudo-robustness) rather than architecture; targeted attacks only partially convincing — these add genuine insight beyond 'models are vulnerable'.

Good reproducibility practices: publicly available checkpoints, standard benchmark dataset (DNS Challenge 4), 20 seeds with standard error reporting, and detailed appendices covering masking computation, PGD projection, and optimization details.
weaknesses: No human listening study (ABX) to substantiate the central 'imperceptibility' claim; the paper leans on an established psychoacoustic model plus a 12 dB safety margin, but prior work cited by the authors itself showed masked perturbations can still be detectable by humans. Given imperceptibility is the core contribution distinguishing this from Dong et al., this is a notable evidentiary gap.

Effectively white-box only: no gradient-free black-box attacks (e.g., estimation or query-based) are attempted, so the practical threat model for real adversaries (e.g., closed-source commercial DNS in videoconferencing) remains untested; conclusions about attack practicality are correspondingly weakened.

Defense evaluation is shallow: only a non-adaptive Gaussian noise baseline is tested; the authors themselves acknowledge adaptive attacks would defeat it. No adversarial training, randomized smoothing, or purification baselines are evaluated, limiting the countermeasure contribution.

Targeted attacks are only partially successful: high STOI to the target does not correspond to audible target speech, so the most severe claimed threat (inducing arbitrary output utterances) is demonstrated only in metric space, not perceptually.

The choice of attack iteration budget was set to equalize wall-clock time (~1 hour per model) rather than convergence, which may disadvantage some models and confounds the model-comparison results (e.g., FSN+ vs. others).

Over-the-air evaluation is fully simulated (convolution with RIRs); the required loosening of the masking constraint (6 dB) introduced audible crackling, further underscoring the need for perceptual validation.

Significance is somewhat bounded by the scope: the paper establishes vulnerability of four specific open-source models; the broader implications (e.g., for deployed systems, streaming settings) remain speculative without further work.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic threat analysis: the paper evaluates four state-of-the-art open-source DNS models (Demucs, Full-SubNet+, FRCRN, MP-SENet) across a wide range of conditions (near-clean 70 dB SNR to noisy, with/without reverb, simulated over-the-air with both synthetic and real recorded RIRs), substantially generalizing prior work (Dong et al.) which covered only 2 models and limited SNR ranges.

Strong methodological rigor in evaluation: five complementary computational metrics (STOI, ViSQOL, NISQA, DNSMOS, Whisper-based word accuracy), a human transcription and ABX study with 15 audio experts, and unusually careful statistics (two-way 'pigeonhole' bootstrap CIs for crossed participant–item effects, intersection–union test for the primary claim) rather than naive significance tests.

Honest and informative negative results: targeted attacks succeed on objective metrics but not subjectively; imperceptible universal perturbations fail; naive cross-architecture and cross-checkpoint transfer fails; FSN+'s apparent robustness is traced to exploding gradients (pseudo-robustness) rather than architecture—these findings are valuable to the community.

Well-motivated technical contributions: psychoacoustic masking with temporal pre/post-masking and a −12 dB offset as a PGD projection operator, plus Wiener-deconvolution/gradient-descent projection for over-the-air perturbations; an ablation cleanly isolating the perceptibility contribution of each pipeline component.

Excellent transparency and reproducibility: online samples and code, detailed appendices (masking computation, OTA optimization, fixed-iteration sanity check, human-study design and statistics), and a full license/compliance table. The compute-standardized attack budget is a thoughtful design choice, and it is validated in Appendix D.6.
Responsible treatment of limitations (white-box requirement, offline per-utterance attacks, real playback-chain nonlinearities unmodeled) and a constructive discussion of implications and defenses.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the attack framework is primarily an adaptation of existing psychoacoustic masking (Lin & Abdulla, Schönherr et al., Qin et al.) and standard PGD to a new target domain; the headline result—that imperceptible adversarial noise degrades DNS models—extends rather than fundamentally challenges expectations from prior audio adversarial work.

Attacks are strictly white-box, offline, and per-utterance; transfer and universal perturbations fail, so the demonstrated practical threat is narrow (an attacker needs gradient access to the exact model and knowledge of the utterance). The safety-critical threat framing in the introduction somewhat outpaces what is actually demonstrated.

Defense evaluation is shallow: only Gaussian noise with a non-adaptive attacker is tested; the authors themselves acknowledge an adaptive attacker would likely circumvent it, so the defense conclusions are preliminary.

Human study is small (15 participants) and drawn from a single industrial research lab where the authors appear to work; participants are audio experts, so imperceptibility to naive listeners is not established. OTA attacks additionally required loosening the masking constraint by 6 dB, producing audible crackling, which weakens the over-the-air imperceptibility claim.

Some evaluation details rely on hand-tuned hyperparameters ('selected by hand through extensive subjective evaluation'), and one OTA attack failing to converge was handled by substituting the unperturbed value, slightly muddying the average results; scale is limited to 20 seeds per condition.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical coverage: four open-source DNS models, ten environmental conditions (SNR × reverb), simulated over-the-air attacks with both simulated and real recorded RIRs, 20 seeds, and a fixed-iteration sanity check (Appendix D.6) that rules out compute-budget confounds.

Triangulated evidence for the central claim: five computational metrics (STOI, ViSQOL, NISQA, DNSMOS, Whisper WAcc), a human transcription study, and an ABX imperceptibility study, with statistically careful analysis (pigeonhole bootstrap, intersection-union test) rather than naive tests.

Honest and thorough treatment of negative results: failed universal perturbations, failed targeted attacks at the subjective level despite objective metric success, and weak transfer are all reported clearly rather than hidden, which strengthens the credibility of the positive claims.

Useful mechanistic finding that Full-SubNet+'s apparent robustness stems from exploding gradients (obfuscated-gradient pseudo-defense) rather than architecture, size, or domain, with a clean ablation (Table 1, fixed-iteration check).

The masking-threshold ablation (Appendix D.4) is well designed: calibrating simpler constraints to matched attack success cleanly isolates the perceptibility cost of each pipeline component, quantifying the value of temporal masking (3.6 dB).
Good reproducibility hygiene: released code and samples, checkpoint versions and commits, license table, and detailed optimization hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The paper positions itself as an extension of Dong et al. [13], but the core method (PGD + psychoacoustic masking, following Qin et al. [38]) is standard; the main contributions are stricter perceptibility constraints, more models, and more settings. This is breadth rather than a new technique, which weakens the technical contribution.

The practical threat model is narrow, which undercuts the security significance emphasized in the abstract. Attacks are white-box (gradients assumed), offline, and per-utterance; universal perturbations, targeted attacks (subjectively), and cross-model transfer all fail. As the paper itself concedes, a streaming or real-world attacker would need capabilities that do not yet exist, so the 'urgent security concerns' framing overstates the demonstrated risk.

Over-the-air experiments are simulation-only (linear RIR convolution). The paper acknowledges that real playback chains introduce nonlinearities, gain control, and codec compression, any of which could break the attack; no physical playback experiment is performed, leaving a major gap between the claimed OTA threat and what is shown.

The defense evaluation is incomplete and non-adaptive. Only Gaussian noise is tested, and the authors note an adaptive attacker would likely circumvent it; standard adaptive attacks against the defense (as required by Tramèr et al. [53], whom they cite) are not attempted, so conclusions about defenses are preliminary.

The human study is small and confined: 15 participants from a single industrial research lab, fixed stimuli shared across participants (only 6 clips per condition), and ABX results that are only 'marginally above chance' with substantial variance. The imperceptibility claim is supported but not strongly, and the sample is not representative of end users.

Some methodological inconsistencies weaken the headline claims: the OTA attacks relax the masking constraint by ~6 dB and produce 'slight crackling' admitted to be audible; one OTA attack that failed to converge was silently assigned its unperturbed score; and MP-SENet inputs were truncated to 5 s due to a known bug, introducing mild non-comparability across models.

Reliance on STOI as both objective and primary metric raises circularity concerns: the attack optimizes STOI and success is largely reported in STOI, and the authors themselves demonstrate that STOI is unreliable for targeted attacks (high STOI without subjective intelligibility). The multi-metric Figure 2 mitigates this, but the headline figures remain STOI-centric.

The 'gradient flow matters more than model size' insight rests on only four models and is essentially an observation that one model exhibits exploding gradients; generalization of this mechanistic claim is unclear.

strengths: First systematic, comprehensive study of imperceptible (psychoacoustically masked) adversarial attacks against deep noise suppression models, generalizing and significantly extending prior work (Dong et al.) along perceptibility, attack goals, and real-world coverage (near-clean to noisy, reverb, simulated over-the-air).

Strong methodological rigor: principled psychoacoustic masking constraint with temporal pre/post-masking and threshold offset, a masking-aware projection operator for PGD, and a thoughtful treatment of the harder over-the-air setting via Wiener deconvolution plus gradient-based projection.

Rare and valuable use of human evaluation: transcription and ABX studies with 15 audio/multimedia experts, with careful statistics (pigeonhole bootstrap for crossed participant-item effects, intersection-union test) rather than naive tests; the human study validates both attack success (unintelligibility) and imperceptibility.

Comprehensive evaluation across four state-of-the-art open-source models, five complementary computational metrics, 20 seeds, multiple SNR/reverb conditions, and real recorded RIRs; compute-standardized attack budgets with a fixed-iteration sanity check to rule out confounds.

Honest and thorough reporting of negative results (no transfer, no effective universal perturbations, targeted attacks that succeed on metrics but not perceptually), which strengthens credibility and provides useful boundaries on the threat model.

Useful mechanistic insight that Full-SubNet+'s apparent robustness stems from exploding gradients (pseudo-robustness) rather than architecture or model size, plus an ablation quantifying the perturbation budget contributed by temporal masking (3.6 dB gap).

Practical significance: clear articulation of threat model and implications for safety-critical DNS deployments (hearing aids, emergency comms), with a preliminary defense analysis; code and samples released, and licenses carefully documented.
weaknesses: Attacks are white-box, offline, and per-utterance; while the authors acknowledge this, the practical threat is narrower than the framing sometimes suggests, especially given that transfer and universal perturbations fail under strict masking.

Over-the-air attacks are simulated (RIR convolution, including real recorded RIRs) rather than physically executed; nonlinear playback-chain effects (gain control, codecs, speaker/mic nonlinearity) are acknowledged but untested, leaving open whether real OTA attacks are feasible.

Human study is small (15 participants, all from a single industrial research lab) and ABX imperceptibility is inconclusive (59% mean accuracy with substantial variance); no IRB review was obtained, and headphone use was recommended but not enforced.

Defense evaluation is minimal: only non-adaptive Gaussian perturbation is tested; the authors themselves note an adaptive attacker would likely circumvent it, and no established defenses (randomized smoothing, purification, adversarial training) are evaluated.
Masking thresholds had to be loosened (6 dB vs 12 dB) for over-the-air attacks, introducing audible crackling, slightly weakening the 'imperceptible' claim in that setting.

Some experimental choices are idiosyncratic: different iteration budgets per model (though justified and sanity-checked), MP-SENet truncated to 5 seconds due to a VRAM bug, and manual/hand-tuned hyperparameters.
